stem:
Table 1 shows census results for a fictional growth point that has become a town in Zimbabwe (fictional data).

| Census year | Population |
|---|---|
| 1992 | 18,400 |
| 2002 | 31,200 |
| 2012 | 46,000 |
| 2022 | 64,400 |

Resource: the town's council reports that a group of shacks has appeared on a stream bank between the high-density suburb and the industrial area, with no piped water or toilets. The town centre has banks, supermarkets and the council offices, and the tallest buildings in the town.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in the town's population between 1992 and 2022.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Which urban zone is described by 'banks, supermarkets, council offices and the tallest buildings'?

options.rationale: Correct: the CBD has the highest land values, so offices and shops build upwards.
This has large plots and big houses, not tall offices.
The fringe mixes farmland and new development on the edge of town.

parts.explanation: Accessibility and high land values give the CBD tall commercial buildings.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Name the urban land-use model in which zones form rings around the CBD.
parts.explanation: Burgess's concentric zone model has rings of land use around the CBD.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Using the resource, describe **three** characteristics of the unplanned settlement.

points.description: Shacks made of temporary or scrap materials.
No piped water or toilets / no services.
Built on unsuitable land (stream bank, liable to flooding) between other zones / unauthorised by the council.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The homes are shacks, there is no piped water or toilets, and they are on a stream bank that may flood, on land not planned for housing.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain the causes of the town's rapid growth.

points.description: Rural-urban migration: push factors in surrounding communal areas (drought, land shortage, few jobs).
Pull factors: jobs in industry, trade, services and the informal sector; better schools and clinics.
Natural increase: young migrants have children in the town.
Government investment as a growth point (roads, electricity, services) attracting business.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: People from surrounding communal areas are pushed by drought and land shortage and pulled by jobs in shops, factories and the informal sector, and by better schools and clinics. Young migrants then have children in the town, and investment in the growth point's roads and electricity attracted businesses.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe **four** effects of rapid urbanisation on a town in Zimbabwe.

points.description: Housing shortages / growth of unplanned settlements / overcrowding and lodgers.
Shortage of water and overloaded sewers / disease outbreaks.
Unemployment and growth of the informal sector / crime.
Traffic congestion, pollution, uncollected refuse / pressure on schools and clinics.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Housing runs short so families take lodgers or build shacks; water supplies and sewers are overloaded; many people cannot find formal jobs and turn to vending; and roads become congested and refuse piles up.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Name **one** high-density and **one** low-density residential suburb in a named Zimbabwean city.

points.description: High-density suburb correctly named (e.g. Harare: Mbare, Highfield, Glen View, Mufakose, Kuwadzana; Bulawayo: Makokoba, Mzilikazi, Nkulumane, Entumbane).
Low-density suburb correctly named (e.g. Harare: Borrowdale, Mount Pleasant, Highlands, Greendale; Bulawayo: Suburbs, Hillside, Burnside).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Harare: Mbare (high density) and Borrowdale (low density).

parts.explanation: One of each, in the same named city.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: With reference to a named urban centre in Zimbabwe, explain the measures that can be taken to solve the problems of unplanned settlements.

points.description: Names an urban centre and an unplanned settlement (e.g. Harare: Epworth or Caledonia).
Upgrading (in situ): water pipes, toilets, roads, electricity in the existing settlement.
Regularisation: giving residents legal title / planning layouts so they invest in better homes.
Site-and-service schemes: serviced plots for self-built houses.
Low-cost housing schemes / cooperatives / building brigades / low-cost loans.
Growth points and rural development to reduce rural-urban migration.
Enforcing planning laws to stop building on unsafe land (wetlands, stream banks).
Evaluates: cost, demand exceeding supply, affordability; judgement on most effective.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Harare has several unplanned or partly planned settlements, such as Epworth on its south-eastern edge. One measure is upgrading the settlement where it stands, by laying water pipes, building toilets and grading roads, which improves health without moving people away from their jobs. Regularisation, in which plots are surveyed and residents receive legal title, encourages families to replace shacks with brick houses. The council can also provide site-and-service schemes, where plots with water and sewer connections are allocated for people to build on, and support housing cooperatives and low-cost loans. Planning laws should be enforced to stop people building on wetlands and stream banks, where floods and disease are a risk. In the long term, developing growth points and rural services reduces the migration that creates unplanned settlements. These measures cost money and demand is greater than supply, so upgrading and regularisation, which are cheaper and keep communities together, are probably the most effective.

parts.explanation: Measures explained with a named Zimbabwean example.

explanation: A ZIMSEC Paper 2 Section C settlement question: urban growth data, land-use zones and models, unplanned settlements and their solutions.
hints: Think of the push and pull factors in Zimbabwe.

stem:
Resource: a description of part of a fictional 1:50,000 map extract of rural Zimbabwe. In the north, homesteads are spread out singly across a gently sloping plateau with sandy soils. In the centre, about thirty homesteads are clustered around a borehole, a school and a clinic. In the south, homesteads are strung out in a line along both sides of a gravel road that follows a ridge. A river with a wide, flat floodplain flows west to east across the extract; there are no homesteads on the floodplain.

On the map, the distance by road from the clustered village to the main road junction measures 4.6 cm.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Which settlement pattern is shown by the homesteads in the south?

options.rationale: Nucleated homesteads are clustered around a central point.
Dispersed homesteads are spread out singly.
Correct: they follow the line of the road along the ridge.

parts.explanation: Linear settlements follow roads, rivers or ridges.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Name the settlement pattern shown by the homesteads in the centre of the extract.
parts.explanation: Homesteads grouped around a borehole, school and clinic form a nucleated pattern.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the distance on the ground from the clustered village to the road junction.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** reasons for the nucleated pattern in the centre of the extract.

points.description: A reliable water supply (the borehole) attracts homesteads.
Services such as the school and clinic are shared / easy to reach.
Security / social ties / planned village layout / scarce water elsewhere.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Families cluster round the borehole for water, and the school and clinic are close by; living together also gives security and community support.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Explain why there are no homesteads on the river's floodplain, and how settlements can be sited and built more safely.

points.description: The floodplain floods in the wet season / cyclones, so homes and lives are at risk.
Settlements should be sited on higher ground, away from rivers and steep unstable slopes.
Disaster-resilient building: strong foundations, raised floors, firmly fixed roofs, strong bridges and drains.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The floodplain is flooded in heavy rains, as happened in the east during Cyclone Idai in 2019, so people build on higher ground. Homes should be away from rivers and steep slopes, with strong foundations and roofs tied down.

parts.label: (f)
parts.stem: Describe **four** challenges caused by rapid growth in a named Zimbabwean city.

points.description: Water shortages and overloaded sewers / water-borne disease (e.g. Harare cholera 2008-2009).
Housing shortages / overcrowding / unplanned settlements (e.g. Epworth).
Traffic congestion in and around the CBD / overcrowded commuter transport.
Uncollected refuse and illegal dumping / unemployment and informal trading / pollution.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In Harare, water supply has not kept pace with growth, so many suburbs depend on boreholes and vendors; housing shortages lead to lodgers and settlements such as Epworth; the CBD is badly congested with minibuses; and refuse is often uncollected.

parts.explanation: Four challenges for a named city.

parts.label: (g)
parts.stem: Suggest **three** ways of reducing traffic congestion in a Zimbabwean city.

points.description: Improve and expand public transport (large buses, commuter trains).
Build bypasses, ring roads or widen roads / improve traffic lights.
Designated ranks and loading zones / park-and-ride / staggered working hours / decentralise services.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Provide more large buses and commuter trains, build bypasses to keep through traffic out of the CBD, and enforce designated ranks for minibuses.

parts.label: (h)
parts.stem: Explain how urban authorities in Zimbabwe can manage rapid urban growth. Refer to a named urban centre.

points.description: Names the urban centre (e.g. Harare or Bulawayo).
Housing: site-and-service schemes, upgrading, low-cost housing, satellite towns (e.g. Chitungwiza, Ruwa).
Water and sanitation: new or repaired treatment works, boreholes, sewer repairs.
Transport: buses, commuter trains, road improvements, managing minibuses.
Waste: regular refuse collection, recycling, controlled landfills.
Jobs: designated vending sites and support for the informal sector; attracting industry.
Rural development / growth points to reduce rural-urban migration.
Evaluates: lack of funds, demand exceeding supply; judgement.

levels.descriptor: Developed, accurate explanation of several relevant points, supported by a located example or the resource, with a clear judgement or conclusion where the question asks for one.
Some explanation of relevant points, partly developed; an example or resource evidence is used in general terms; any judgement is simple or one-sided.
Simple statements or a list of points with little explanation; no example or only a name.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Harare has grown far faster than its services. To manage housing, the council can provide site-and-service plots and upgrade informal areas, while satellite towns such as Chitungwiza and Ruwa take some of the population. Water treatment works and sewers need repair and expansion, with boreholes as a short-term supply. Congestion can be reduced with more large buses and commuter trains, bypasses and designated ranks for minibuses. Regular refuse collection, recycling projects and controlled landfill sites reduce illegal dumping and disease. Designated vending sites give informal traders space without blocking pavements. In the long term, developing growth points and rural services reduces rural-urban migration. These measures all need money, which councils often lack, so priority should go to water and sanitation, which protect public health.

parts.explanation: Management strategies explained with a named Zimbabwean centre.

explanation: A ZIMSEC Paper 2 Section C settlement question: rural settlement patterns and siting from a described map, scale, urban challenges and management.
hints: At 1:50,000, 1 cm on the map = 0.5 km on the ground.
Think about why people avoid the floodplain.
